sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Two contracting methods are used for permanent soil nail walls, alone or combined: the procedural or method approach, where the contract documents specify all details of design, materials and methods (example specification in Appendix E), and the performance or end-result approach, where they specify the criteria for a successful outcome and the design is submitted with the construction drawings (Appendix F). The choice depends on project criticality and complexity, the Owner's experience and specialty contractor availability. Specifying drilling and grouting methods is not recommended.
sections.body: 8.1 Introduction (p. 225). Two types of contracting methods can be used to develop contract drawings and specifications for permanent soil nail walls; some Owners prefer one or a combination. The method is selected based on the criticality and complexity of the project, the experience of the Owner and its consultants, and the availability of specialty contractors; both are valid if properly implemented. Procedural or Method Approach: all details of design, construction materials and methods are specified in the contract documents (example specification in Appendix E). Performance or End-Result Approach: the contract documents specify the criteria for the successful outcome; a full design and detailing and the construction methods are not prescribed, and a detailed design submittal accompanies the construction drawings (example in Appendix F). Because specialty contractors often introduce innovative, cost-competitive solutions, contract documents should let them use the latest techniques: specifying the drilling and grouting methods or other means and methods is not recommended under either approach, although restrictions can exclude undesirable methods in given subsurface conditions. The example specifications in Appendices E and F carry italic comments to help tailor them.
key_points: Procedural or method approach: design, materials and methods all specified (Appendix E)
Performance or end-result approach: outcome criteria specified; design submitted with construction drawings (Appendix F)
Selection by project criticality and complexity, Owner experience, specialty contractor availability
Do not specify drilling and grouting methods; restrictions on undesirable methods are acceptable
Both approaches need the three geotechnical analyses of Section 8.2
sections.applicability: Choosing a contracting approach for permanent soil nail walls.

sections.title: Geotechnical Analyses Required by Specifications
sections.summary: Under either approach three analyses are essential to the feasibility assessment: global stability, deformation, and soil corrosivity/corrosion protection class. They may be in the geotechnical report, done by the Owner, or required from the Contractor, who then needs ample bid time. The Owner should give the Contractor its stability results and soil parameters, conduct deformation evaluations where deformation is critical, and test corrosivity before bid documents, specifying the corrosion class and design life.
sections.body: 8.2 (pp. 225-227). Whether the procedural or performance approach is followed, three essential analyses must be conducted as part of the feasibility assessment: global stability, deformation, and soil corrosivity/corrosion protection class determination. They may be part of the geotechnical report in the contract documents, performed by the Owner, or required submittals from the Contractor; if required of the Contractor, the bid documents must allow ample time for its own investigation and analyses. Global stability: the Owner may do its own stability analyses and wall design before bid (recommended for Owners with sufficient expertise and local experience); if it leaves the design to the Contractor, it should provide its stability results and disclose all issues, while requiring the Contractor to verify stability; if the Contractor performs the global stability analyses, the specifications must say so and the Owner should provide soil shear strength parameters, pore pressures and similar information, and time in the bid. Deformation: where deformation is not critical, the Owner may perform preliminary analyses; where it is critical, the Owner should always conduct deformation evaluations and set in the performance specifications the minimum considerations (and any required numerical methods) for the Contractor's analysis, and the minimum monitoring methods. Corrosivity: before bid documents, the Owner must perform corrosivity testing on representative samples (Chapter 4) to determine the corrosion class; the class and design life are generally specified by the Owner and shown on the plans; test results should always be given to the Contractor, who may substitute a higher class.
key_points: Three analyses under either approach: global stability, deformation, corrosivity/corrosion protection class
By the Owner (in the geotechnical report) or required Contractor submittals, with ample bid time
If the Contractor does global stability, the Owner should provide shear strength, pore pressure and other data
Critical deformation: Owner always evaluates and sets minimum considerations and monitoring methods
Corrosivity testing by the Owner before bid documents; Owner specifies corrosion class and design life
Owner provides corrosivity results; Contractor may substitute a higher corrosion class
sections.applicability: Geotechnical analyses and corrosivity testing required in soil nail wall contract documents.

sections.title: Experience Requirements for Contractors
sections.summary: A satisfactory installation is more likely with an experienced, qualified soil nail Contractor with experienced personnel and good QC, and with comprehensive QA enforced by the Owner; Owners new to soil nailing should use a competent third-party QA provider. Contract documents should define experience requirements (minimum experience duration and/or number of similar projects, extending to drillers and nozzlemen), their submittal and enforcement; typical requirements are in Appendices E and F. Some public Owners may not pre-qualify contractors by law.
sections.body: 8.3 (p. 227). The Contractor's practices need to provide a high quality product and avoid conditions that jeopardize the wall or endanger workers. Barring differing conditions, a satisfactory installation is more likely when an experienced and qualified soil nail Contractor with experienced personnel and good QC procedures is selected, regardless of the construction method, and more so when comprehensive construction quality assurance procedures are developed and enforced by the Owner or the inspection personnel. Owners with no previous soil nailing experience should seek a competent third-party quality assurance provider. Contract documents should clearly define the Contractor experience requirements, the submittal procedures for this information, and how the Owner will enforce them, as many transportation Owners do for ground anchor walls, micropiles, drilled shafts and shotcreting. Some public Owners are prohibited by law from pre-qualifying contractors, which does not preclude requiring bidders to demonstrate specific soil nail experience. The requirements must extend to specialized personnel (drillers, nozzlemen) and include a minimum duration of experience with similar work and/or a minimum number of projects with similar soil nail walls; typical requirements are in the guideline specifications of Appendices E and F.
key_points: Experienced, qualified Contractor with good QC increases the likelihood of a satisfactory installation
Owner-enforced QA; Owners new to soil nailing should use a third-party QA provider
Contract documents define experience requirements, their submittal and their enforcement
Requirements cover specialized personnel: minimum experience duration and/or number of similar projects
Some public Owners cannot pre-qualify contractors but can require demonstrated experience
Typical experience requirements: guideline specifications in Appendices E and F
sections.applicability: Contractor and personnel experience requirements in soil nail wall specifications.

sections.title: Procedural Specifications
sections.summary: The procedural approach provides detailed plans and specifications so every bidder prices a defined product and bids compare easily. It needs Owner staff trained in soil nail design and construction, who are then an asset during construction. The Owner is fully responsible for the design and performance, provided the Contractor builds strictly to the documents, and assumes the design risks and the cost of modifications. It is recommended only for Owners with sufficient in-house expertise.
sections.body: 8.4 (p. 228). The procedural approach develops a detailed set of plans and specifications for the bidding documents, so that each bidder has a defined product to price and the Owner can compare pricing more easily. It lets the Owner's engineers examine design options but requires staff trained in soil nail wall design and construction methods, who then become a valuable asset during construction when questions or design modifications arise. The Owner is fully responsible for the design and performance of the soil nail system as long as the Contractor installs each component (nails, facing, drainage) in strict accordance with the contract documents; the Owner assumes all design risks and the modifications and costs required by actual field conditions, and should provide existing geotechnical reports as reference documents. A procedural or method specification is recommended only for Owners who have developed sufficient in-house expertise and consider soil nail wall design and construction control a conventional or standard method of earth retention.
key_points: Detailed plans and specifications: every bidder prices a defined product
Needs Owner staff trained in soil nail design and construction; they help during construction
Owner fully responsible for design and performance if the Contractor builds to the documents
Owner assumes the design risks and field-driven modifications and costs
Recommended only for Owners with sufficient in-house expertise
sections.applicability: Procedural (method) contracting for Owner-designed soil nail walls.

sections.title: Performance-Based Specifications
sections.summary: In the performance approach (line and grade, conceptual plans, Design/Build) the Owner defines geometry, aesthetics and materials, performance requirements (LRFD resistance factors, corrosion protection levels, deformation limits) and acceptable methods; an experienced designer for the Contractor designs the wall. Owner costs fall, but its engineers need the expertise to review the design or a consultant. Bids are lump sum or unit price per square foot of face. Recommended for Owners with limited soil nail experience or complicated projects.
sections.body: 8.5 (pp. 228-230). Often called line and grade, conceptual plans or Design/Build. The Owner (i) prepares drawings defining the geometric and aesthetic requirements and material specifications, (ii) defines performance requirements including LRFD resistance factors, corrosion protection levels and deformation limits, and (iii) indicates the range of acceptable design and construction methods. With sound specifications and contractor experience requirements, the design by an experienced designer (in-house or retained by the Contractor) suits the Contractor's equipment and methods, and the Owner's preconstruction engineering costs drop; the disadvantage is that the Owner's engineers must have the expertise to review the design and approve modifications, or engage a proficient consultant. Bid quantities come from pay limits on the line and grade drawings, on a lump sum or unit-price basis per square foot of wall face. Special provisions should give the basis for special designs, the submittals (Contractor calculations and design drawings, shop drawings and construction processes, material information) with their schedules and review, and construction control and monitoring. The Owner furnishes: plan of the areas to be retained; typical cross sections; elevations; utilities and other structures and their loads; construction constraints; external loads; drainage limits; tolerable seismic deformations and the design ground motion return period where applicable; governing design manual sections and acceptable design methods; results of all geotechnical investigations and testing (or a baseline geotechnical report); maximum resistance factors and material limits; corrosion protection level; face aesthetics; alignment tolerances and allowable horizontal movements; percentage of nails tested, procedures and acceptance criteria; and monitoring requirements. If the geotechnical information is not to be relied upon, the Contractor needs ample time to investigate. Performance specifications are recommended for Owners with limited soil nail experience or for complicated projects where a specialty Contractor's knowledge can be maximized.
key_points: Also called line and grade, conceptual plans or Design/Build
Owner defines geometry, aesthetics, materials, performance requirements and acceptable methods
Performance requirements include LRFD resistance factors, corrosion protection levels and deformation limits
Owner's engineers must be able to review the design, or engage a proficient consultant
Bid as lump sum or unit price per square foot of wall face, from line and grade pay limits
Owner furnishes geotechnical results (or a baseline report), resistance factor limits, corrosion level, testing and monitoring requirements
Recommended for Owners with limited soil nail experience or complicated projects
sections.applicability: Performance-based (Design/Build) contracting where the Contractor's designer designs the soil nail wall.
